assessmentSummary.identity: A two-hand medicine-ball rotational wall throw preceded by a declared lateral shuffle or crow-hop that creates momentum into a controlled plant, pivot, projection, and finish.
currentCardFindings: The two active legacy cards describe the same lateral-shuffle-to-rotational-medicine-ball projection and are a direct identity collision.
The current 40-versus-50 overall difficulty split is unsupported seed drift; both names preserve the same approach, projection, and intent.
Neither legacy source fixes the return contract, so the legacy baseline variants remain archived provenance rather than being guessed into throw-only or rebound-catch.
Planned versus reactive cueing changes decision demand and must be explicit; it does not change the primary movement identity.
Five direct YouTube candidates currently return healthy oEmbed metadata, but no full viewing or human approval has occurred.

variantDifficultyCandidates.basis: the athlete coordinates a lateral approach, plant, pivot, rotational projection, and balanced finish without a required returning catch
the same dynamic approach and projection add return tracking, catch timing, and whole-body absorption

proposedLoadProfile.recoveryHours: context dependent; combine with lateral acceleration, change-of-direction, rotational throwing, shoulder, elbow, trunk, plant, and catch exposures

proposedConstraints.groupRule: One active thrower per lane; waiting athletes and collectors stay outside approach, pivot, flight, and return space.
proposedConstraints.clinicalBoundary: Pain, instability, recent injury or surgery, neurologic symptoms, or rehabilitation restrictions require individualized clinician guidance.

proposedDosage.effort: high intent only while shuffle rhythm, plant, sequence, release speed, target, balance, and any prescribed catch remain repeatable
proposedDosage.ballRule: Use the lightest ball that produces the intended ballistic action; reduce mass if speed, sequence, posture, plant, target, or catch control worsens.
proposedDosage.sideRule: Declare approach and throw side and balance high-intent repetitions unless a documented reason says otherwise.
proposedDosage.stopRule: End the set on the first symptom, lane issue, plant failure, target loss, material output decline, uncontrolled spine motion, unpredictable return, or missed catch.

proposedFatigueRecovery.acuteCost: moderate neural and whole-body ballistic cost with low metabolic demand at output dosage; rebound catch and reactive cueing add perceptual demand
proposedFatigueRecovery.recoveryRule: Do not repeat high-intent exposure while pain, soreness, approach or plant error, target loss, release-speed decline, balance loss, or catch hesitation persists.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Use a declared lateral shuffle or crow-hop to create momentum into a controlled plant, whole-body rotational two-hand medicine-ball projection to an inspected wall, and balanced finish. The exact variant states whether the athlete retrieves the ball or tracks and absorbs a predictable rebound.

population.clinicalBoundary: Symptoms, instability, recent surgery, neurologic signs, or rehabilitation restrictions require individualized clinician guidance.
population.selectionBoundary: Select the exact return contract, approach, throw side, ball, target, distance, cueing, and dose from current readiness and intent; exercise cards do not carry proficiency levels.

evidence.sourceTitle: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw Video Exercise Guide
claims: The exact exercise source names a shuffle into rotational medicine-ball throw and describes an athletic base, trail-hip load, one lateral shuffle, rotational wall projection, and optional rebound catch.
Shuffle-to-Rotational Medicine Ball Throw is the stable broad identity. The two legacy names describe the same lateral-shuffle-to-rotational-projection sequence.

evidence.sourceTitle: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw Video Exercise Guide
claims: The defining sequence combines lateral locomotion, whole-body rotation, two-hand ballistic projection, and controlled deceleration.
Shuffle count, throw side, wall target, return contract, planned or reactive cue, and ball specification must be explicit delivery dimensions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Analysis of trunk muscle activity in the side medicine-ball throw
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Side medicine-ball throwing recruits trunk musculature during rapid rotation and force transfer.
The lateral approach adds foot, ankle, knee, hip, and frontal-plane stabilization demands to the trunk, shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand demands of the rotational projection.

evidence.sourceTitle: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw Video Exercise Guide
claims: The exact source describes loading the trail hip, shuffling once, driving from the back leg, transferring weight, rotating around the front leg, and throwing into a wall.
Observable mechanics are a controlled lateral gather, stable plant, ground-to-hip-to-trunk-to-hand sequence, complete release, target accuracy, balanced finish, and the declared reset or catch.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Rotational medicine-ball output can be compared only with standardized load, direction, technique, and measurement.
Exercise complexity and physical difficulty are scored independently; overall difficulty is their maximum. No athlete proficiency label belongs on an exercise card.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of seated and standing throwing velocity using differently weighted medicine balls
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Medicine-ball mass and throwing technique materially change release velocity.

Shuffle-to-Rotational Medicine Ball Throw adds lateral acceleration, plant and pivot, rotational projection, deceleration, and—when prescribed—visual tracking and rebound absorption to cumulative training budgets.

evidence.sourceTitle: 8 Creative Ways to Use a Medicine Ball
claims: Ball construction and wall interaction determine rebound behavior and catch feasibility.
The setup must declare a medicine ball, inspected wall, lane width and length, approach direction, plant zone, target, distance, floor traction, traffic boundary, and return path.
NSCA classifies explosive medicine-ball throws with maximal-effort alactic work and multi-minute recovery rather than fatigue circuits when power is the objective.
Use short side-balanced sets, full resets, and enough recovery to preserve approach rhythm, plant control, release speed, target accuracy, and any prescribed catch.

evidence.sourceTitle: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw Video Exercise Guide
claims: The sequence is athletic base, load trail hip, one lateral shuffle, drive and rotate around the front leg, project to the wall, then reset or catch as declared.
The athlete cue should remain short: load, shuffle, plant, turn from the ground up, throw through the target, own the finish.

evidence.sourceTitle: Medicine Balls: An ACE Integrated Fitness Training Model Workout
claims: A returning catch requires predictable rebound behavior and whole-body absorption.
Stop for pain, neurologic symptoms, unsafe footing or lane intrusion, uncontrolled plant or spine motion, target loss, output decline, unpredictable return, or missed catch.
Explosive medicine-ball work is freshness-sensitive and should be separated from fatigue-dominant work when maximal intent is required.
Shuffle-to-Rotational Medicine Ball Throw belongs early in an output block or in a controlled technique block; planned and reactive cueing must not be silently interchanged.

evidence.sourceTitle: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw Video Exercise Guide
claims: Athlete support should show start mark, shuffle direction and count, throw side, plant zone, ball, wall target, return contract, primary cue, and stop signal.
Offer static rotational throw, shorter approach, lighter ball, throw-only, larger target, and longer reset options without assigning an exercise skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Measurement requires a standardized ball and exact protocol.
Coach support must expose side, approach, ball, wall, distance, target, return contract, dose, rest, observation angle, quality errors, output metric, fatigue signal, and lane shutdown.

evidence.sourceTitle: 8 Creative Ways to Use a Medicine Ball
claims: Ball rebound and catch demand are equipment- and participant-dependent.

Accessibility options include a lighter or softer ball, high-contrast target and floor marks, reduced approach, throw-only delivery, fewer repetitions, longer reset, plain-language text, and non-video instructions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw Video Exercise Guide
claims: Shuffle-to-rotational medicine-ball throw and medicine-ball shuffle-to-rotation throw are naming aliases for one identity.

Return contract is an exact variant; shuffle count, approach distance, ball mass, target, and planned cue are modifiers. Static, step-behind, scoop, shot-put, slam, partner-reactive, and bound-to-throw tasks require separate identity or variant review.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The five links are discovery candidates with currently healthy oEmbed metadata only. Full viewing, exact sequence and return-contract match, safety, captions, accessibility, reviewer identity, and approval remain unresolved.

alternateAssessments.name: Med Ball Shuffle-to-Rotation Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: The legacy name preserves the same lateral-shuffle approach and rotational medicine-ball projection.

alternateAssessments.name: Shuffle Into Rotational Medicine Ball Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: This is the common naming order for the same movement sequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Shuffle Rotational Wall Throw — Throw and Retrieve
alternateAssessments.rationale: The defining approach and projection end after release without a required catch.

alternateAssessments.name: Shuffle Rotational Wall Throw — Rebound and Catch
alternateAssessments.rationale: The same approach and projection add a predictable return and controlled catch.

alternateAssessments.name: Reactive Shuffle-to-Rotational Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: A visual or verbal cue changes decision demand and side selection but preserves the primary movement sequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Static Rotational Medicine Ball Wall Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing the lateral approach preserves the projection but materially lowers locomotion, plant, timing, and spacing demand.

alternateAssessments.name: Step-Behind Rotational Medicine Ball Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: Step-behind footwork changes approach sequencing and plant geometry.

alternateAssessments.name: Lateral Bound to Rotational Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: A bound adds aerial projection, landing impact, and single-leg absorption before the throw.

alternateAssessments.name: Shuffle-to-Rotational Scoop Toss
alternateAssessments.rationale: A low-to-high scoop path changes implement position, release angle, and shoulder action.

alternateAssessments.name: Shuffle-to-Shot-Put Throw
alternateAssessments.rationale: A unilateral shot-put release changes arm use, ball position, laterality, and shoulder demand.

alternateAssessments.name: Shuffle-to-Rotational Slam
alternateAssessments.rationale: A floor-directed slam changes target, projection direction, impact, and retrieval.

alternateAssessments.name: Partner-Reactive Shuffle Rotational Pass
alternateAssessments.rationale: A trained partner and reactive return alter cueing, target behavior, communication, and catch logistics.
